body:
What is haemoglobin?

Haemoglobin (Hb) is an iron-containing protein present in red blood cells, also called erythrocytes. It gives blood its characteristic red colour and plays a central role in transporting oxygen from the lungs to body tissues.

Human red blood cells normally contain large amounts of haemoglobin. The haemoglobin molecules bind oxygen where it is abundant, particularly in the lungs, and release oxygen to tissues where it is needed for cellular respiration.

Cellular respiration releases usable energy from nutrients. An adequate supply of oxygen is therefore essential for the normal functioning of many body tissues.

How haemoglobin transports oxygen

Oxygen enters the lungs during inhalation and passes into the blood across the walls of the lung's air sacs and nearby capillaries.

Oxygen binds reversibly to haemoglobin in red blood cells. Blood then carries oxygen through the circulation to body tissues, where oxygen is released and can enter cells.

Haemoglobin also contributes to carbon dioxide transport, although much of the carbon dioxide in blood is carried in the form of bicarbonate.

What does a haemoglobin reading mean?

A haemoglobin test measures the concentration of haemoglobin in a given volume of blood. The result is commonly reported in grams per decilitre (g/dL).

A reading of 14 g/dL means that the blood contains approximately 14 g of haemoglobin per 100 mL.

Normal haemoglobin ranges vary with sex, age, pregnancy, altitude and laboratory reference standards. There is no single range that applies to every person.

Common adult haemoglobin reference ranges

MedlinePlus, a service of the US National Library of Medicine, provides the following general adult laboratory reference ranges:

Adult groupTypical haemoglobin range
Men13.8–17.2 g/dL
Women12.1–15.1 g/dL

These are examples of laboratory reference intervals, not universal limits. The reference range printed on a particular laboratory report may differ slightly.

What is anaemia?

Anaemia is a condition in which the haemoglobin concentration is below the appropriate threshold for a person's population group, reducing the blood's capacity to carry oxygen adequately.

Anaemia may cause tiredness, weakness, dizziness, paleness or shortness of breath. However, symptoms vary according to severity and cause, and mild anaemia may produce few noticeable symptoms.

Iron deficiency is an important cause of anaemia, but it is not the only cause. Blood loss, inadequate vitamin B12 or folate, certain chronic diseases and inherited blood disorders can also produce anaemia.

WHO haemoglobin thresholds for anaemia

The World Health Organization issued updated haemoglobin cutoffs in its 5 March 2024 guideline.

For adults aged 15–65 years, the following thresholds apply to the specified groups:

Population groupAnaemia threshold
Men, 15–65 yearsBelow 13.0 g/dL
Nonpregnant women, 15–65 yearsBelow 12.0 g/dL
Pregnancy, first trimesterBelow 11.0 g/dL
Pregnancy, second trimesterBelow 10.5 g/dL
Pregnancy, third trimesterBelow 11.0 g/dL

These values are anaemia cutoffs rather than complete normal laboratory intervals. WHO guidance also provides adjustments and considerations for factors such as altitude.

For example, haemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL is below the WHO anaemia threshold for a nonpregnant adult woman aged 15–65 years. A haemoglobin result of 12.8 g/dL is below the WHO anaemia threshold for an adult man in the same age range.

Reference interval versus anaemia threshold

A laboratory's typical normal interval and a public-health anaemia cutoff serve different purposes. They should not be treated as identical numerical boundaries.

Why adequate haemoglobin matters

If haemoglobin concentration becomes too low, the blood's ability to transport oxygen decreases. Body tissues may receive less oxygen than they require, especially during increased physical activity.

Adequate production of haemoglobin depends on healthy red blood cell formation and the availability of nutrients such as iron. Folate and vitamin B12 are also important for normal red blood cell production.

A balanced diet containing appropriate sources of these nutrients contributes to maintaining healthy blood formation. However, dietary changes alone may not correct every cause of anaemia.

Haemoglobin and HbA1c are different measurements

The abbreviation Hb usually refers to haemoglobin when discussing an ordinary haemoglobin concentration test.

HbA1c refers to glycated haemoglobin and is used to assess average blood glucose over approximately 2–3 months.

MeasurementMain purposeUnit
Haemoglobin (Hb)Assess oxygen-carrying protein concentration and possible anaemiag/dL
HbA1cAssess longer-term blood glucose exposure%

A person may have low haemoglobin without diabetes, or diabetes without low haemoglobin. The 2 measurements must not be confused.

Indian public-health connection: Anaemia Mukt Bharat

Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) is an Indian public-health initiative addressing anaemia among important population groups, including children, adolescents and women.

Its interventions include iron and folic acid supplementation, nutritional awareness, haemoglobin testing, appropriate treatment and attention to non-nutritional causes of anaemia.

The National Health Mission's programme information, updated on 3 August 2026, continued to list Anaemia Mukt Bharat and its testing and prevention activities. The information describes programme interventions rather than providing a new national anaemia prevalence estimate for 2026.

One-glance revision of health measurements

The measurements covered in this lesson describe different properties of the body or food. A useful way to revise them is to connect each measurement with its unit and most important recognition threshold.

Blood pressure and haemoglobin both relate to blood circulation but measure different properties. BMI relates body weight to height. Blood glucose measures circulating sugar, while GI describes the relative glucose response associated with carbohydrate-containing foods.

Correct interpretation begins by identifying what is being measured, which unit is used, and which reference standard applies.

Prelims focus

  • Haemoglobin is an iron-containing oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells.
  • Haemoglobin concentration is commonly expressed in g/dL.
  • Typical adult laboratory ranges are approximately 13.8–17.2 g/dL for men and 12.1–15.1 g/dL for women.
  • WHO 2024 anaemia cutoff for men aged 15–65 years: below 13.0 g/dL.
  • WHO 2024 anaemia cutoff for nonpregnant women aged 15–65 years: below 12.0 g/dL.
  • Trap: Haemoglobin concentration and HbA1c are different tests with different units and purposes.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 11, Transportation in Animals and Plants, section 11.1, pp. 121–123, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Biology, Class 11, Body Fluids and Circulation, section on erythrocytes, GPSC Biology compendium Volume 34, pp. 105–107; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia, Hemoglobin, Normal Results and What Abnormal Results Mean, US National Library of Medicine, consulted 3 November 2026; World Health Organization, Guideline on Haemoglobin Cutoffs to Define Anaemia in Individuals and Populations, 5 March 2024, Tables 2 and 3; US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, A1C Test for Diabetes and Prediabetes, consulted 3 November 2026; National Health Mission, Anaemia Mukt Bharat, programme information updated 3 August 2026, consulted 3 November 2026.]
